Unquenched large orbital magnetic moment in NiO

S. K. Kwon and B. I. Min Address:  Department of Physics, Pohang University of Science and Technology, Pohang 790-784, Korea
February 22, 2000
Abstract

Magnetic properties of NiO are investigated by incorporating the spin-orbit interaction in the LSDA + UU scheme. It is found that the large part of orbital moment remains unquenched in NiO. The orbital moment contributes about μL=0.29​μB\mu_{L}=0.29\mu_{B} to the total magnetic moment of M=1.93​μBM=1.93\mu_{B}, as leads to the orbital-to-spin angular momentum ratio of L/S=0.36L/S=0.36. The theoretical values are in good agreement with recent magnetic X-ray scattering measurements.

pacs
PACS number: 71.20.Be, 71.70.Ej, 75.10.Lp, 75.50.Ee

]

Electronic and magnetic structures of late 3​d3d transition metal (TM) mono-oxides (MnO, FeO, CoO, and NiO) have been extensively investigated over the last decades [1]. Conventional band theory with the local spin density approximation (LSDA) fails to describe the electronic structures of the compounds. In the LSDA calculations, the energy gaps of MnO and NiO are underestimated[2]. Even worse, FeO and CoO are predicted to be metallic which are, on the contrary, large gap insulators in nature. The main problem in the LSDA is the use of mean field-type exchange-correlation functional which is improper to describe localized 3​d3d electrons.

There have been several theoretical efforts to cure the deficiencies in the LSDA, for example, the self-interaction correction (SIC) scheme [3, 4, 5], the GW approximation (GWA) [6, 7], and the LSDA + UU method [8, 9]. The SIC-LSDA is in the line of the extended LSDA by removing unphysical electron interaction with itself. In the GWA, the quasi-particle energy is obtained through the self-energy calculation to the lowest order in the screened Coulomb interaction WW. The GWA method applied to NiO gives a rather good description of the energy gap size [7]. Computational load, however, is very heavy in the GWA. The LSDA + UU method overcomes the failure of the LSDA by incorporating the on-site Coulomb correlation UU of the multiband Hubbard model-like. In this method, localized 3​d3d electrons are treated separately from delocalized s​psp electrons. As a result, all the 3​d3d TM mono-oxides in the LSDA + UU are obtained as insulators with well developed energy gaps which are comparable to experimental values [8]. In this way, the energy gap problem in 3​d3d TM mono-oxides is considered to be solved by various calculational methods.

Due to the outermost characteristics of TM 3​d3d electrons, atomic 3​d3d orbitals are greatly deformed in solids by the crystal field and/or band hybridization effects. Hence, the orbital moment of 3​d3d TM ion is usually quenched in solids, because it originates from atomic nature of involved atomic elements[10]. For example, all the 3​d3d ferromagnetic transition metals of Fe, Co, and Ni show negligible orbital magnetic moments in the range of μL≲0.1​μB\mu_{L}\lesssim 0.1\mu_{B} [11]. It is, however, expected that the strong Coulomb correlation in 3​d3d TM mono-oxides preserves the orbital moment of localized 3​d3d electrons by reducing the ligand crystal field effects at metal ion sites.

In fact, for CoO, it is easily conceived that the orbital moment is only partially quenched because the measured magnetic moment M=3.4​μBM=3.4\mu_{B} [12] simply exceeds the spin magnetic moment alone and the minority t2​gt_{2g} band is occupied only two-thirds of its available states. Therefore, the existence of orbital moment in CoO has been stressed many times [2, 5, 13]. It is also shown that the LSDA + UU method gives a good description of magnetic structure of CoO with a large orbital moment of μL∼1​μB\mu_{L}\sim 1\mu_{B} [14]. On the other hand, in the case of NiO, measured magnetic moments are in the range of M=1.77∼2.2±0.2​μBM=1.77\sim 2.2\pm 0.2\mu_{B} [15, 16, 17], which are comparable to the spin only moment of isolated Ni2+ ion. Therefore, the magnetic moment in NiO has been fully attributed to the spin moment and the orbital moment is expected to be completely quenched.

However, recent magnetic X-ray scattering measurement [17] indicates that the orbital-to-spin angular momentum ratio in NiO is as large as L/S=0.34L/S=0.34, far from fully quenched orbital moment. In the nonresonant magnetic X-scattering, the separation of spin and orbital moment is possible, because the spin and orbital moment densities have different geometrical prefactors in the scattering cross section that can be adjusted by changing either the scattering geometry or the X-ray polarization. In Ref. [17], the orbital moment in NiO is extracted by the polarization analysis of nonresonant magnetic-scattering intensities. This method has evidenced a large contribution of the orbital moment to the total magnetic moment. They also found that the spin and orbital moments in NiO are collinear.

Magnetic moment is one of the basic ground state quantities which should be provided by an appropriate band method. If the orbital moment is so large in NiO, all the previous attempts [8, 18, 19] which tried to directly compare calculated spin moments with experimental moments are under a mistake. The linearized muffin-tin orbital (LMTO) calculation for NiO with an orbital-polarization (OP) correction (LSDA + OP) in a crystal-field basis yields the spin and orbital magnetic moments of μS=1.43​μB\mu_{S}=1.43\mu_{B} and μL=0.12​μB\mu_{L}=0.12\mu_{B}, respectively [20]. Although the total magnetic moment is significantly improved to M=1.55​μBM=1.55\mu_{B} with the OP correction, as compared to M=1.23​μBM=1.23\mu_{B} from the LSDA, it is still smaller than the experimental measurements and the ratio of L/S=0.17L/S=0.17 is only half of the magnetic X-ray scattering value [17]. The SIC-LSDA method [5] yields a large orbital moment of μL=0.27​μB\mu_{L}=0.27\mu_{B}, which, however, was suspected as a methodological artifact by other authors [8, 18]. In more recent study, the orbital moment is simply neglected [19].

To determine the size of orbital moment in NiO, we have performed the LSDA + UU calculations using the LMTO band method within the atomic sphere approximation (ASA). The incorporation of the spin-orbit coupling into the LSDA + UU method is known to give right orbital polarization in strongly correlated electron systems [14]. The LSDA + UU Hamiltonian is given by

ℋL​S​D​A+U=ℋL​S​D​A−ℋd​c+ℋU{\cal H}_{{\mathrm{L}SDA}+U}={\cal H}_{\mathrm{L}SDA}-{\cal H}_{\mathrm{d}c}+{\cal H}_{U} (1)

where the first term in the right hand side is the LSDA Hamiltonian and the second term is the double counting correction for the third term ℋU{\cal H}_{U}. With the Coulomb interaction UU and exchange interaction JJ parameters, one can write ℋd​c{\cal H}_{\mathrm{d}c} and ℋU{\cal H}_{U}, respectively, as

where nm​m′σn_{mm^{\prime}}^{\sigma} is the dd occupation number matrix of spin σ\sigma and Nσ=T​r​(nm​m′σ)N^{\sigma}={\mathrm{T}r}(n_{mm^{\prime}}^{\sigma}), N=N++N−N=N^{+}+N^{-}. We relate the screened Coulomb interaction V⁡(m​m′,m′′​m′′′)V(mm^{\prime};m^{\prime\prime}m^{\prime\prime\prime}) with the Slater integral FkF^{k};

V⁡(m​m′,m′′​m′′′)=∑k=02​lck​(l​m,l​m′′)​ck​(l​m′,l​m′′′)​Fk,\displaystyle V(mm^{\prime};m^{\prime\prime}m^{\prime\prime\prime})=\sum_{k=0}^{2l}c^{k}(lm,lm^{\prime\prime})c^{k}(lm^{\prime},lm^{\prime\prime\prime})F^{k}, (4)

where ck​(l​m,l​m′)c^{k}(lm,lm^{\prime}) is a Gaunt coefficient. For 3​d3d electrons, three Slater integrals of F0,F2F^{0},F^{2}, and F4F^{4} are involved in the calculation. Among those, the ratio of F4/F2F^{4}/F^{2} is known to be constant ∼0.625\sim 0.625 for most 3​d3d TM atoms [21]. Hence, the actual number of parameters is reduced from three FkF^{k}’s to two of UU and JJ, which are given by U=F0U=F^{0} and J=(F2+F4)/14J=(F^{2}+F^{4})/14, respectively. To determine the orbital moment, the spin-orbit coupling is simultaneously included in the self-consistent variational loop [11]. We have assumed the antiferromagnetic ordering state of type-II, and the experimental lattice constant of a=7.893a=7.893 a.u. is used.

In Fig. 1, magnetic moment behavior is shown with varying the lattice constant in the LSDA. Both the spin and orbital magnetic moments increase monotonically with increasing the lattice constant. This feature is understandable in view of that the crystal field strength at Ni sites and the hybridization between Ni 3​d3d and O 2​p2p bands are reduced with volume expansion. At the experimental lattice constant of a=7.893a=7.893 a.u., the spin and orbital magnetic moments are obtained as μS=1.12​μB\mu_{S}=1.12\mu_{B} and μL=0.15​μB\mu_{L}=0.15\mu_{B}, respectively, which are consistent with existing results [20]. Both the spin and orbital magnetic moments are larger in NiO than in fcc Ni which has μS=0.63​μB\mu_{S}=0.63\mu_{B} and μL=0.06​μB\mu_{L}=0.06\mu_{B}. This suggests that 3​d3d electrons are more localized in NiO than in Ni metal. Although the ratio of L/S=0.27L/S=0.27 in the LSDA is only slightly smaller than L/S=0.34L/S=0.34 in the experiment (see Table. 1), the spin and orbital polarizations in the LSDA are not large enough because of underestimation of the Coulomb correlation between 3​d3d electrons.

Figure 2 shows the Coulomb correlation effects on the magnetic moments obtained by the LSDA + UU method. We have used the exchange parameter of J=0.89J=0.89 eV which is comparable to literature value [8]. Once the strong Coulomb interaction is introduced between Ni 3​d3d electrons, the magnetic moments increase substantially. The role of the Coulomb interaction is significant to localize Ni 3​d3d electrons. With U=8.0U=8.0 eV found in Ref. [8] and Ref. [22], we have obtained the spin and orbital magnetic moments of μS=1.64​μB\mu_{S}=1.64\mu_{B} and μL=0.29​μB\mu_{L}=0.29\mu_{B}, respectively. The total magnetic moment M=1.93​μBM=1.93\mu_{B} and the ratio L/S=0.36L/S=0.36 for U=8.0U=8.0 eV are in good agreement with the experimental data. The change of the Coulomb parameter UU by 1.01.0 eV results in increments of both the magnetic moments and the ratio L/SL/S by Δ​μS∼Δ​μL∼0.01​μB\Delta\mu_{S}\sim\Delta\mu_{L}\sim 0.01\mu_{B} and Δ⁡(L/S)∼0.01\Delta(L/S)\sim 0.01, respectively. The overall total magnetic moment difference and the ratio L/SL/S difference are only Δ​M=0.12​μB\Delta M=0.12\mu_{B} and Δ⁡(L/S)=0.05\Delta(L/S)=0.05 inbetween U=6.0U=6.0 and 1010 eV. Thus, all the magnetic moments and the ratio L/SL/S are rather insensitive to the Coulomb interaction UU within the employed parameter range.

Calculated magnetic moments are summarized in Table. 1 in comparison with experimental data and previous results by other calculational methods. As mentioned above, the sizes of magnetic moments are underestimated in the LSDA. The total magnetic moment of M=1.27​μBM=1.27\mu_{B} in the LSDA is much smaller than M=1.77∼2.2±0.2​μBM=1.77\sim 2.2\pm 0.2\mu_{B} in experiments [15, 16, 17]. In the LSDA + OP, the spin moment is significantly improved to μS=1.43​μB\mu_{S}=1.43\mu_{B} [20], which, however, is still smaller than the experimental values. More serious is the decrease of orbital moment in the LSDA + OP, which unfavorably makes the consistency between the theoretical and experimental L/SL/S ratio become worse. Both the SIC-LSDA (M=1.80​μBM=1.80\mu_{B}) [5] and the LSDA + UU (M=1.93​μBM=1.93\mu_{B}) give values in agreement with experimental data. But it can be concluded that the LSDA + UU results with U=8.0U=8.0 eV and J=0.89J=0.89 eV, among various calculations, are especially in best agreement with experimental measurements. The ratio of L/S=0.36L/S=0.36 in the LSDA + UU is also consistent with L/S=0.34L/S=0.34 in the magnetic X-ray scattering measurement [17].

In conclusion, we have found using the LSDA + UU calculations that the orbital moment in NiO is not fully quenched, which is as large as μL=0.29​μB\mu_{L}=0.29\mu_{B}. Both the total magnetic moment of M=1.93​μBM=1.93\mu_{B} and the orbital-to-spin angular momentum ratio of L/S=0.36L/S=0.36 for U=8.0U=8.0 eV are close to experimental values. The Coulomb correlation and the spin-orbit coupling are crucial to get right magnetic polarization in NiO.
